To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sym 5 mutant of pea nodulates poorly at high root temperatures, that this can be overcome by lowering the temperature, and that a short cool period, early in the process of nodulation, is sufficient to stimulate nodulation of sym 5 mutants.
the sym 5 mutant of Pisum sati- vum L. is temperature-sensitive for nodule formation.
the nodulation of Pisum sativa L. homozygous mutants (sym 5), is temperature-sensitive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the gene(s) involved in the nodulation process in pea (Pisum) and with the elucidation of the mechanisms involved.
the identification of the gene responsible for the sym 5 phenotype and the characterization of the gene product.
the identification of the genes and the mechanisms involved in the nodulation of Pisum satvum L.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sym 5 gene controls a step in the infection process which is sensitive to temperature.
the nodulation defect of sym 5 is temperature‐sensitive and can be rescued by a short period of low temperature.
the nodulation process of sym 5 mutants is temperature-sensitive and that a cool period early in the infection period is sufficient to increase nodulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a temperature‐sensitive mutation in pea (sym 5), which affects a 66-kD protein (Sym 5), is responsible for a temperature‐dependent change in nodulation.
sym 5 mutants have an altered nodulation response that is sensitive to temperature.
the sym 5 mutant of Pisum satvum L. has a defect in the regulation of nodulation by root temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sym 5 gene is involved in a signal transduction pathway, which is temperature sensitive.
the temperature-sensitivity of the sym 6 mutants can be used to increase nodulation of the sym 8 mutants.
temperature is an important variable for studying the molecular basis of nodulation.
